nodes.name: The Improvement Manifesto
nodes.summary: John Glennane's 2026 declaration for human-centred improvement: business should lead technology, and original, complete, durable “True Design” should replace templates and quick fixes.
nodes.detail: A visual call to move beyond accidental improvement, technocratic ready-made answers, AI shortcuts, and “best practice.” Its preferred alternative is agency, human vocation, trust, and Next Practice.
keyIdeas: Improvement should begin with human purpose and business need—not with a technology looking for a use case.
Templates and borrowed “best practices” can suppress original thinking and create accidental, incomplete change.
True Design should be original, coherent and durable enough to survive beyond the launch moment.
The manifesto argues for Next Practice: learning forward from context rather than copying yesterday’s answer.
nodes.whyItMatters: A strong provocation for transformation leaders: AI and automation can accelerate change, but they cannot substitute for judgement, agency and a genuinely designed operating model.

nodes.name: Make Boards Work
nodes.summary: Marc O. Stöckli's practical guide to moving boards from legally required bodies to vital sources of judgement, challenge, trust, and strategic value.
nodes.detail: The book combines behavioural norms—beginner's mind, psychological safety, and trust—with board composition, conflicts, the chair as lightning rod, and a disciplined cycle before, during, and after meetings.
keyIdeas: A board creates value through the quality of its collective judgement, not through compliance theatre or ceremonial meetings.
Composition matters, but behaviour matters just as much: curiosity, candour, trust and psychological safety determine whether expertise can be used.
The chair shapes the conditions for productive challenge and acts as a lightning rod when interests or personalities collide.
Board effectiveness is a cycle spanning preparation, the meeting itself, follow-through and continuous reflection.
nodes.whyItMatters: Useful as a practical diagnostic for any leadership team that is formally impressive but operationally weak: it connects governance structure with the human dynamics that make challenge constructive.

nodes.name: The Emperor
nodes.summary: Tarot archetype of authority, structure, stability, boundaries, and disciplined leadership.
nodes.detail: Jim shared Biddy Tarot's interpretation of the fourth Major Arcana card: a figure of order, protection, disciplined authority and the structures that make stability possible.
keyIdeas: Upright, The Emperor represents authority, leadership, structure, boundaries and the capacity to turn intention into order.
Its constructive form is protective and dependable: rules and systems create a stable platform for others.
Its shadow is rigidity—control becoming domination, certainty suppressing learning, or structure becoming an end in itself.
As a leadership prompt, the card asks where firmer boundaries are needed and where authority has become too inflexible.
nodes.whyItMatters: A compact symbolic lens for leadership conversations: healthy authority supplies clarity and safety, while unhealthy authority confuses control with strength.

nodes.name: The Circle
nodes.summary: Dave Eggers' 2013 dystopian novel about a dominant technology company whose pursuit of transparency erodes privacy, autonomy, and dissent.
nodes.detail: Mae Holland joins the Circle, a powerful technology company combining search, social identity, payments and surveillance. What begins as convenience and belonging gradually becomes a system in which visibility is treated as virtue and privacy as guilt.
keyIdeas: Convenience can become coercive when opting out carries social or professional punishment.
Radical transparency sounds democratic while concentrating power in the platform that owns the data and rules.
Participation metrics turn relationships, identity and even morality into performance.
The novel’s central warning is not only surveillance, but how willingly people trade autonomy for belonging, safety and frictionless service.
nodes.whyItMatters: Still relevant to AI and platform governance: a system can be useful, popular and apparently benevolent while quietly eliminating the space required for privacy, dissent and independent judgement.

nodes.name: On Bullshit
nodes.summary: Harry Frankfurt's philosophical essay distinguishing bullshit from lying: the liar tracks truth in order to conceal it; the bullshitter is indifferent to truth.
nodes.detail: Harry Frankfurt’s short philosophical essay argues that bullshit is not simply falsehood. A liar must respect the truth enough to hide it; the bullshitter is focused instead on producing an impression and is indifferent to whether the claim is true.
keyIdeas: Lying and bullshit are different relationships to truth: concealment versus indifference.
Bullshit grows where people are expected to speak with authority about matters beyond their knowledge or evidence.
The speaker’s real subject is often the speaker—the image of competence, sincerity or certainty they want to project.
Because it weakens concern for truth itself, bullshit may be more corrosive than an identifiable lie.
nodes.whyItMatters: A precise tool for reading corporate language, political rhetoric and AI-generated confidence: ask whether the claim is trying to describe reality or merely engineer an impression.

nodes.name: The Basic Laws of Human Stupidity
nodes.summary: Carlo M. Cipolla's satirical model of stupidity: people routinely underestimate its prevalence and destructive power, especially when actions harm others without benefiting the actor.
nodes.detail: Carlo M. Cipolla presents five mock-serious laws and a two-axis model of human behaviour. The dangerous category is the stupid person: someone whose action creates losses for others while producing no gain—and often a loss—for themselves.
keyIdeas: We consistently underestimate how many stupid people are active in any population or institution.
Stupidity is independent of status, education, wealth or profession; competence in one domain offers no immunity.
Cipolla maps behaviour by gains and losses to self and others: intelligent, bandit, helpless and stupid.
Stupid actors are uniquely dangerous because their behaviour is irrational, unpredictable and difficult to bargain with.
nodes.whyItMatters: A funny but memorable risk lens: systems should not assume every harmful act has a rational incentive. Robust organisations must also withstand behaviour that destroys value for everyone.

nodes.name: Those Magnificent Men in Their Flying Machines
nodes.summary: The 1965 British adventure comedy about an eccentric international air race from London to Paris in the pioneering era of aviation.
nodes.detail: Set in 1910, the film follows an eccentric international field of aviators competing in a London-to-Paris air race. Their fragile machines, rivalries, romances and national stereotypes turn technological progress into elaborate comic chaos.
keyIdeas: Early aviation appears as both engineering breakthrough and magnificent improvisation.
The race becomes a theatre of national character, personal vanity, courage, cheating and accidental cooperation.
Its pleasure lies in physical spectacle: eccentric aircraft, practical stunts and machines that only barely work.
Beneath the comedy is affection for pioneers who accept absurd risk before a technology becomes ordinary.
nodes.whyItMatters: A playful companion to innovation discussions: every mature system once passed through a stage of unreliable prototypes, colourful characters and brave experiments.
